Martin Luther, living from fourteen eighty-three to fifteen forty-six, was a German Augustinian friar, theologian, and priest whose critique of the Roman Catholic Church's practices, particularly the sale of indulgences, sparked the Protestant Reformation and fractured Western Christianity. By nailing his Ninety-five Theses to the church door in Wittenberg in fifteen seventeen and defending his positions against papal authority, Luther initiated a religious revolution that reshaped European theology, politics, and society.

Martin Luther was born in Eisleben in Saxony, Germany. He became an Augustinian monk and earned a doctorate in theology at the University of Wittenberg, where he became a professor of biblical studies. Luther's theological breakthrough came through studying the biblical book of Romans and the concept of sola fide, or "faith alone." He concluded that salvation comes through faith in Christ alone, not through works or sacramental mediation by the Church—a conviction that contradicted Catholic teaching.

In fifteen seventeen, Luther composed his Ninety-five Theses, a scholarly critique of papal indulgences, the Church's practice of selling remission of sin to raise funds. Though composed as an invitation to academic debate, they were translated, printed, and disseminated across Europe within weeks. Luther's public conflict with the papacy escalated. He refused to recant his positions at the Diet of Worms in fifteen twenty-one before the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, declaring "Here I stand, I can do no other"—a defiant moment that became legendary in Protestant tradition.

Luther was excommunicated by Pope Leo X in fifteen twenty-one. He subsequently translated the Bible into German, completed in fifteen thirty-four, making scripture accessible to common people and establishing him as a founder of biblical scholarship and Protestant theology. Luther emphasized sola scriptura, or "scripture alone," and sola fide, rejecting papal authority, priestly intermediaries, and many Catholic sacraments and practices. He advocated for a simplified church governed by local princes and scripture rather than Rome.

Luther married Katharina von Bora, a former nun, in fifteen twenty-five—a defiant act against clerical celibacy that symbolized Protestant rejection of Catholic moral hierarchy. This established the Protestant clergy as married, ordinary people rather than a separate caste. Luther's ideas were translated into political reform by German princes who broke from Rome. His theology profoundly influenced the emergence of Protestantism across Northern Europe and permanently split Western Christianity.
